Enjoy this long post of the use of reverb...

REVERB
The main purpose of reverb is to introduce a defined sonic space for each instrument/the whole track. We are used to hearing sounds in a particular environment, always. Recorded sound generally seeks to be no different... but the rules are certainly looser.

No digital reverb algorithms attempt to model the PRECISE path of all of your signal's sound waves. It's all rough tricks to make your brain perceive a certain set of dimensions and stereo separation.

You can deliberately take advantage of the listener's expectations, by utilising your own tricks with reverb to achieve many odd effects.

There are some producers who record everything as 'dry' as possible... Close mics and dead recording spaces, or recording synths straight to DAW, then they don't add any digital reverb at all. The ostensive reason for this is that they wish their tracks to sound as 'in your face' as possible. It sounds very synthetic and odd. Artistically, you might like it for some sounds. However, I usually add a minuscule amount of ambient reverb to all my sounds of recent. To have anything wholly dry is to make it stand out in an odd fashion to my ears.

It is a good idea to mix reverb on headphones... this will make it a lot more apparent what is going on because you don't have the environment of your listening room to confuse you. Headphones have intimacy and clarity.

*Note from commenters: due to the stereo effects of reverb, monitors are also recommended when mixing reverb, as headphones will not accurately depict the nature of stereo imaging like monitors can.

I am very fond of Lexicon Native for drums sounds... and the vastly cheaper alternatives are ValhallaVintageVerb and ValhallaRoom. ValhallaVintageVerb is great for instrument reverbs... both the Valhalla verbs are good for drum sounds but you have to tweak a lot. Lexicon Native has some GREAT presets.

BASIC CONTROLS
Mix: It's very obvious what it does!... but remember that 100% wet can be used for many things, as a very unusual effect, or a basis to chop up/reverse, filter etc.
Pre-Delay: the first reflections of your sound in a room, largely dictate what size that room appears to your brain, as the first reflection will bounce off the closest notable surface... Pre-delay creates a gap before any reverberating signal appears... the longer that gap, the larger the room will feel. Having no pre-delay can make drums feel a bit stifled by the verb... they can lose some impact... but most other instruments don't necessarily need pre-delay.

Decay: this is the length of your reverb tail. Utilising as small a decay as e.g. 0.2secs, can still place your sound into an useful ambient space. If you wish to use very long verbs, consider automating the 'mix' control in its own track to prevent bleed into the wrong sections.
Size: This changes the reverb algorithm to better imitate the appropriate dimensions. A larger room will have a lower 'echo density', as the reflections have further to travel. High frequency (HF) gets preferentially attenuated by propagating through air. So, the larger a room, the more quickly the HF will disappear in relation to the decay.

Utilising the filters on your reverb can change the perceived size of the room mildly, beyond the basic EQ and 'feel' changes. Brighter = smaller, and vice versa.

Do not feel limited to obeying realism, but here is the simplest rule. A smaller room will have a smaller pre-delay and a smaller decay... and vice versa.

A note on 'mix' levels. Higher 'mix' settings can effectively take the listener 'further away' (and less direct - imagine being next to the mouth of a cave, with a sound reverberating inside... that's about the closest you'll get to 100% wet in reality) from the sound source. Lower mix settings place the listener at the source of the sound.

I am fond of using reverb as an artistic tool, as well as in subtle amounts, purely for spatial concerns. You can have reverb on a send from a channel, then process it however you wish, filter it, add distortion, collapse it to mono... the possibilities are vast. Use different reverbs for different instruments. Be very careful with the verb on a kick drum; a reverb that can be fine for every other instrument can create a kick drum that sounds ridiculously boomy.

DRUM REVERB
Standard drum reverb needs to have decent initial echo density. The reverb should mostly sound like a reinforcing repeat, like slap-back echo. A long tail won't generally add the correct 'feel' to drums, it'll take away rhythm/impact. 'Gating' a long tail is a way of getting an extreme initial verb sound, that quickly disappears, so as to still add to the rhythm. Very '80s and synthetic sounding.

I like to bounce a 100% reverb of each drum hit. Then add my own envelope to the waveform afterwards. You can do any form of your own 'gating' this way.

Plate reverbs sound great on drums. Particularly snares. Snares are toms sound the most natural with heavier verb. As noted, your kick will lose impact/sound odd if too washy, so being more subtle can work better. I don't like adding much verb to hats and percussion, because HF is meant to be attenuated to such a degree that higher mix levels of sizzly verb sounds bizarre to my ears.

You may wish to try adding an 'ambient'/spatial verb to your drums (maybe the whole kit)... then add an 'effect' reverb on top (different perhaps for each individual drum track) which feels like more of a slap-back echo, or gated verb.

An ultra ninja trick that I perform is to use the 100% wet reverb from a different drum, over the tail of a sample. This can be a different version of the same percussion instrument, or a different type of percussion verb altogether! So, you could have the reverb from a mellow kick sample playing over an aggressive kick... Or an EQ'd snare reverb playing after a kick etc etc. You may be imagining that this might sound bizarre but it works brilliantly!

INSTRUMENT REVERB
As noted earlier, I tend to utilise a short reverb on all instruments/samples, which you can set up as a send, on its own 'FX channel'. My own ambient settings (to memory) are a 4-8% mix, 5ms pre-delay, 0.40sec decay, 40-70% or so room size (every verb will sound different though).

When creating longer, 'character verbs' for an instrument, be aware that it can be as washy as you think still sounds correct to your ears. Once again though, if the sound is meant to be percussive, like a plucked bass or chord stabs - washy probably is a bad plan. If you are putting reverb onto a lead instrument, the higher the reverb-mix will make the instrument sound less prominent... higher settings will push the lead down in the mix, lower settings make it stand out.

You can do even more bizarre things with instrument reverb than you can get away with on drum reverb. Utilise it as another instrument entirely. Break the perceived rules. Record some 100% wet reverb from some chord/vocal hits and reverse it. Put an envelope on it and use that sound to 'suck' into those chords rhythmically. You can also do this on drums of course, but too much of it, by either volume or occurrence, can detract from the beat, whereas you can truly go bonkers with other instruments. Take a listen to how everything in reversed-reverb sounds... cymbals are amazing for example. You can do further effects on the results you get from reverse verb. Distort, but crush, add echo etc etc.
